Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders

obsessions and compulsions · insight · related disorders · first-line treatmentDoes the repeated act neutralize an unwanted thought?

1Script2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Illness script
Bottom line
  • Obsessions (intrusive, unwanted, ego-dystonic thoughts or images) neutralized by compulsions that take more than 1 hour a day or cause impairment: obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), even when the images are violent
  • First line: exposure and response prevention (ERP) and/or a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI), often at higher doses; clomipramine second line; antipsychotics only augment; buspirone and benzodiazepines do not treat it
  • Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (OCPD) is ego-syntonic perfectionism with no obsessions; a tic has no obsession behind it

DSM-5 lists OCD separately from the anxiety disorders, grouped with its related disorders: body dysmorphic disorder, hoarding disorder, trichotillomania (hair-pulling disorder) and excoriation (skin-picking) disorder

What it is

Intrusive, unwanted thoughts, urges or images (obsessions) and repeated acts or mental acts performed to neutralize them (compulsions); either or both

Driver

A compulsion temporarily relieves the distress an obsession causes, so the ritual repeats

Associated

Tic disorders and Tourette syndrome; trichotillomania; major depressive disorder, which raises suicide-attempt risk

Chain

Obsession anxiety or distress compulsion brief relief

Insights

Are violent intrusive images a sign of psychosis or danger? No: images the patient finds horrifying and tries to neutralize are ego-dystonic obsessions; treat the OCD, not with an antipsychotic alone

Does absent insight make it a psychotic disorder? Not by itself: OCD can be specified with absent insight (delusional beliefs), though most patients recognize their beliefs are not realistic

2Urgent risks
Suicide riskSuicidal thoughts are common in OCD; the risk of an attempt rises with major depressive disorder

If OCD is diagnosed or treated, choose screen for suicidal ideation and depression.

PostpartumNew intrusive fears of contaminating or harming the baby

If delusions or hallucinations are present, choose treat as postpartum psychosis: hospitalization and antipsychotics.

3Differential
Look-alikes, most tempting first
DiagnosisFingerprintDurationDecides it
Psychotic disorder Often delusional beliefs; thoughts held as trueSchizophrenia: 6 months or moreOCD usually recognizes the thoughts as irrational but cannot control them
Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (OCPD)Preoccupation with order, perfectionism and control that slows tasksPresent by early adulthood; persistsEgo-syntonic; no compulsions in response to obsessions
Generalized anxiety disorder Worry, usually about real-life problems such as finances, health and familyAt least 6 monthsWorry, usually without the irrational quality or the rituals of OCD
Tic disorder or Tourette syndrome Sudden, generally involuntary movements or soundsTourette syndrome: over 1 yearNo obsession behind the act; give both diagnoses when they co-occur
Illness anxiety disorder (hypochondriasis) Fear of having a disease, with reassurance seeking6 monthsConcerns restricted to health and disease
Major depressive disorder Rumination mistaken for obsessionAt least 2 weeksRuminations follow a depressed theme
Related disorders
DisorderCore behaviorTreatment
Body dysmorphic disorderPreoccupation with a minor or imagined defect in appearance; mirror checking; repeated cosmetic treatment; insight usually poor or absentSSRIs and/or CBT (cognitive-behavioral therapy)
Hoarding disorderCannot discard possessions regardless of their value; clutter makes living areas unusableCBT; an SSRI trial if CBT fails
Trichotillomania (hair-pulling disorder) Pulls out hair despite trying to stop; not driven by obsessionsCBT (habit reversal)
Excoriation (skin-picking) disorderRecurrent skin picking that causes lesions; not driven by obsessions or appearance concernsHabit reversal and/or an SSRI
4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext move
Violent or sexual images the patient finds horrifying, cancelled by a mental ritualOCDAn SSRI and ERP; not an antipsychotic alone
Contamination fear with repeated handwashingOCDERP and/or an SSRI
New mother with fears of contaminating or harming the babyPostpartum OCDERP and/or an SSRI; delusions or hallucinations point to psychosis
Rigid perfectionism that delays tasks, seen as correctOCPDPsychotherapy (psychodynamic or CBT); SSRIs
Tics alongside obsessionsTic-related OCDSpecify tic-related OCD (step 6)
Cannot discard possessions; cluttered, unsafe homeHoarding disorderCBT first (Related disorders, step 3)

Pause point. The bait: an antipsychotic for violent intrusive images. Images the patient finds horrifying and tries to neutralize are obsessions, not psychosis; start an SSRI with ERP, and keep antipsychotics for augmenting an SSRI.

5Diagnostic criteria
OCD Obsessions – intrusive, unwanted thoughts, urges or images the patient tries to suppress or neutralize · Compulsions – repeated acts or mental acts driven by an obsession or by rules applied rigidly, not realistically connected to what they aim to prevent, or clearly excessive · Time – over 1 hour a day, or distress or impairment · Exclusion – not a substance, medication or medical condition
Specifiers Insight – good or fair, poor, or absent (delusional beliefs) · Tic-related – a current or past tic disorder
6Severity
Measure and specify
FindingAction
Symptom severityRate it with the Yale-Brown Obsessive-Compulsive Scale (Y-BOCS); aim for under 1 hour a day and minimal interference
Poor or absent insightStill OCD: record the insight specifier
Current or past ticsSpecify tic-related
7Treatment
1

First lineOCD diagnosed

ERP and/or an SSRI such as sertraline or fluoxetine How it worksGraded exposure to the triggers of the obsessions while the patient refrains from the rituals DosingOCD often needs a higher SSRI dose than depression; an SSRI is preferred over clomipramine for its adverse-effect profile; many experts combine ERP and medication, especially when severe AvoidBuspirone and lorazepam do not treat obsessions and compulsions
2

Full trialan SSRI is started

Allow 8 to 12 weeks in all before judging it, at least 4 to 6 of them at the top tolerated dose
3

Switchno response to an adequate trial

A different SSRI, or combine medication with ERP
4

Second lineat least two SSRIs have failed

Clomipramine, a strongly serotonergic tricyclic, or venlafaxine Adverse effectsClomipramine is a second-line agent because of its adverse-effect profile
5

Augmentinadequate response to an SSRI

Add an atypical antipsychotic such as risperidone or aripiprazole; not indicated as monotherapy
8Follow-up
Follow-up decisions
WhenDo
The SSRI worksContinue at least 1 to 2 years, if not indefinitely
The patient wants to stopTaper over several months; resume the dose if symptoms worsen
Throughout treatmentRepeat the suicide and depression screen in step 2 (Urgent risks)
Practice
  1. 28-year-old man has unwanted images of pushing strangers onto train tracks Horrified, he avoids platforms and silently repeats a prayer to cancel each image No hallucinations; the rituals take two hours a day → Start an SSRI → Ego-dystonic violent images cancelled by a mental ritual for over an hour a day are OCD; an SSRI with ERP is first line, antipsychotics only augment an SSRI, and anxiolytics do not treat obsessions and compulsions
  2. 41-year-old accountant keeps missing deadlines because she redoes reports until every detail is perfect She insists coworkers follow her lists and will not delegate She sees her standards as correct and has no intrusive thoughts or rituals → Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder → Pervasive perfectionism and control that she sees as correct, with no obsessions or compulsions, is OCPD; OCD is ego-dystonic
  3. 67-year-old man cannot throw away old newspapers and mail, even items of no value Stacks fill his kitchen and hallway, so he cannot cook, and a fall hazard is noted He feels distress at the idea of discarding anything → Hoarding disorder → Difficulty discarding possessions regardless of their value, with clutter that makes living areas unusable or unsafe, is hoarding disorder, treated first with CBT
  4. 24-year-old woman with OCD started sertraline at a low dose 3 weeks ago Her checking rituals have eased slightly; she has no adverse effects She asks whether the drug is failing and wants to try something else → Increase the sertraline dose and continue the trial → OCD often needs a higher SSRI dose than depression, and a trial should continue for 8 to 12 weeks, with at least 4 to 6 of them at the top tolerated dose
  5. Three weeks after delivery, a 30-year-old woman has repeated images of drowning her baby in the bath She knows the images are senseless, avoids bathing the infant, and checks on her often at night No hallucinations or unusual beliefs → Obsessive-compulsive disorder → After delivery, OCD commonly takes the form of fears of contaminating or harming the baby; she knows the thoughts are irrational, unlike a patient with psychosis
  6. 35-year-old man with severe contamination fears has had full trials of fluoxetine and sertraline Each reached the highest tolerated dose for 12 weeks, alongside ERP He still washes his hands for 3 hours a day → Clomipramine → After adequate trials of at least two SSRIs, clomipramine, a strongly serotonergic tricyclic, is a second-line option; antipsychotics only augment an SSRI, and anxiolytics do not treat OCD
  7. 19-year-old man is convinced his nose is crooked, though others see nothing wrong He checks mirrors for hours, has seen three plastic surgeons, and skips class He has no other repeated rituals or intrusive thoughts → Body dysmorphic disorder → Preoccupation with an imagined defect in appearance, with mirror checking and repeated cosmetic visits, is body dysmorphic disorder; it is treated with SSRIs and/or CBT
Pairs with Tics and Tic Disorders: tic-related OCD and exposure and response prevention. Hair Loss in a Child: trichotillomania. Panic Disorder and Other Anxiety: generalized anxiety disorder. SSRI Adverse Effects: adverse effects of the first-line drugs.
Transferable rule

If a repeated act neutralizes an unwanted thought, it is a compulsion: treat with ERP and an SSRI. If the patient sees the rigid trait as right, think of OCPD.
